History and Physical (H&P – Super Detailed)

Consult Summary:
36-year-old man with no past medical history presents via telehealth with 4-day history of severe headache followed by subjective fever, diffuse myalgias, and a blanching pruritic generalized rash after recent travel to Thailand with multiple mosquito bites; requires urgent in-person evaluation to exclude travel-related arboviral infection (e.g., dengue) or other serious febrile illness.

History:
• Presenting complaint: Severe, “very bad” headache for 4 days.  
• Timeline:  
  – Day 0: Headache onset.  
  – Day 1–2: Subjective fever (“feel hot”), not formally measured.  
  – Day 3–4: Diffuse red, itchy, blanching rash noted over entire body; persistent generalized muscle aches.  
• Progression: Headache persists despite paracetamol and ibuprofen (minimal relief). Fever subjectively ongoing; no report of improvement.  
• Associated symptoms:  
  – Myalgias (generalized).  
  – Feels cold at times; no rigors/shivering.  
  – Rash as above.  
• Pertinent negatives:  
  – No photophobia.  
  – No neck pain/stiffness.  
  – No nausea or vomiting.  
  – No cough, coryza, or ear pain.  
  – No focal weakness or paresthesias; able to perform daily tasks.  
• Exposures: Returned from Thailand ~1 week ago; multiple mosquito bites; travel companion also unwell.  

Past Medical History:
• No chronic medical conditions reported.  
• No prior surgeries reported.  
• Immunizations, prior hospitalizations: not discussed.

Medications:
• Paracetamol – dose/route/frequency not documented (as needed for headache).  
• Ibuprofen – dose/route/frequency not documented (as needed for headache).  
• No regular prescription medications.

Allergies:
• Denies drug allergies.

Social History:
• Recent travel: Thailand, returned ~1 week ago.  
• Smoking, alcohol, recreational drugs, occupation, living circumstances: not discussed.

Family History:
• Not discussed.

Physical Examination:
• Telehealth visit – no vitals or physical findings obtained.  
• Patient reports rash that blanches with glass test.

Investigations:
• None performed to date.

Assessment & Plan:
Issue 1 – Febrile headache with diffuse rash after tropical travel  
Assessment: Concerning for mosquito-borne viral illness (dengue fever most likely; chikungunya and malaria also in differential); meningitis less likely but must be excluded clinically.  
Plan:  
  – Urgent same-day face-to-face assessment at GP hub for full physical exam (including vitals, neurological and dermatologic exam).  
  – Consider immediate referral to hospital emergency department if in-person GP assessment unavailable.  
  – Anticipate investigations: CBC with platelets, LFTs, malaria thick/thin smear & rapid antigen test, dengue NS1/IgM/IgG, chikungunya serology/PCR, blood cultures, basic metabolic panel; consider lumbar puncture only if meningitis suspected on exam.  
  – Symptomatic relief: continue paracetamol/ibuprofen as needed (avoid NSAIDs if thrombocytopenia confirmed).  
  – Safety-net advice: seek emergency care for worsening headache, non-blanching rash, bleeding, confusion, neck stiffness, persistent vomiting, or inability to keep fluids down.  

Issue 2 – Rash, generalized pruritus  
Assessment: Likely viral exanthem associated with underlying febrile illness; currently blanching and non-petechial.  
Plan: Monitor; antipruritic measures (e.g., oral antihistamine) if needed after in-person evaluation.

Issue 3 – Travel health / infection control  
Assessment: Possible communicable arboviral illness.  
Plan:  
  – Advise patient to avoid further mosquito exposure (repellent, long sleeves, nets).  
  – Encourage hydration.  
  – Counsel regarding limited use of NSAIDs until platelet count known.  

Summary of Differential Diagnoses (from DDx):
1. Dengue fever – High likelihood: classic triad of fever, severe headache, myalgias; blanching rash appears days 3-5; recent Thai travel with mosquito bites.  
2. Chikungunya virus infection – Moderate likelihood: similar exposure and symptom complex; absent severe arthralgia makes it slightly less likely.  
3. Malaria (P. falciparum) – Moderate likelihood: endemic area travel; headache, fever, myalgias; rash atypical but must be ruled out.

Quality checks:
• Missing expected elements: objective vitals, full systems review, social history details (smoking/alcohol), immunization status.  
• Conflicts noted: Clinician addressed patient as “Ben” at end, while patient identified as “John Doe.”  
• Transcript quality: Clear overall; minor conversational overlaps, no significant inaudible sections.
